readerTitle: Why a 5-cent bag fee works and a 5-cent bonus doesn't
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Homonoff 2018 비닐봉지 세금 vs 보너스, Kahneman·Knetsch·Thaler 1990 머그컵 실험) + 가상 적용 (사내 팀 근무제 변경). 이 개념은 같은 금액의 반전이 핵심이라 company_story 대신 numbers_twist로 바꿨습니다.
insight: 같은 금액이라도 '잃는 것'으로 보이면 '얻는 것'보다 훨씬 강하게 행동을 바꾼다. 그래서 무엇을 주느냐만큼 무엇을 빼앗는 것처럼 보이느냐가 중요하다.
misconception: 금액이 같으면 할인이든 추가 요금이든 고객 반응도 같다. 혜택을 하나 없애도 비슷한 가치의 혜택을 주면 사람들은 공평하다고 느낀다.

sources.text: Homonoff, T. (2018). Can Small Incentives Have Large Effects? The Impact of Taxes versus Bonuses on Disposable Bag Use. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 10(4).
Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk. Econometrica.
Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1992). Advances in Prospect Theory. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty.
Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. & Thaler, R. (1990). Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem. Journal of Political Economy.
Gal, D. & Rucker, D. (2018). The Loss of Loss Aversion. Journal of Consumer Psychology.

factChecks.note: Homonoff(2018): 워싱턴 D.C.의 봉지당 5센트 세금은 일회용 봉지를 쓰는 고객 비율을 40%포인트 이상 줄였고, 메릴랜드 몽고메리 카운티 등 비교 지역의 장바구니 5센트 보너스는 거의 효과가 없었다는 내용. 정확한 수치와 비교 지역 설정을 논문 원문으로 확인하세요.
'손실이 같은 크기의 이득보다 약 두 배 강하게 느껴진다'는 Tversky & Kahneman(1992)의 추정치(λ≈2.25)에 근거합니다. 연구마다 값이 달라 카드에는 'roughly twice'로만 적었습니다.
머그컵 실험: 머그를 받은 사람이 요구한 판매 가격이 사려는 사람의 지불 의사 가격의 약 두 배였다는 결과. 원문 수치(중앙값 약 $7 vs 약 $3 안팎)를 확인하세요. 카드에는 'about twice'로 적었습니다.
Watch out 카드의 학계 논쟁은 Gal & Rucker(2018)를 근거로 일반적인 수준에서만 서술했습니다.

cards.title: Same five cents. Opposite results.
body: Two places near Washington, D.C., tried to get shoppers to stop taking disposable bags. Both used exactly five cents.
One charged five cents for every disposable bag. The other paid shoppers five cents for every reusable bag they brought. On paper, it's the same deal.

image.label: Two checkout counters, one with a 5-cent fee sign and one with a 5-cent reward sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나란히 있는 두 개의 마트 계산대. 왼쪽 계산대에는 "−5¢ per bag" 표지판과 비닐봉지, 오른쪽에는 "+5¢ for your own bag" 표지판과 장바구니. 실제 마트 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which one changed shopping habits more?
body: A five-cent fee per disposable bag, or a five-cent bonus per reusable bag. The money is identical.
Which do you think cut disposable bag use more?

options.text: The bonus. People respond better to rewards than to penalties
options.feedback: Rewards feel friendlier and avoid annoying customers. But in this study the bonus barely moved behavior.

options.text: About the same. Five cents is five cents
options.feedback: That's what a calculator says. It misses how differently people feel about paying versus earning the same amount.

options.text: The fee, by a wide margin
options.feedback: Right. The fee cut disposable bag use sharply, while the bonus did almost nothing. Next card shows why.

cards.title: The fee worked. The bonus barely registered.
body: Economist Tatiana Homonoff studied both policies. After D.C. started charging the fee, the share of shoppers taking a disposable bag fell by **more than 40 percentage points**.
The five-cent bonus for reusable bags had almost no effect. Shoppers simply ignored a small gain.
Nothing about the bags, the stores or the amount explains the gap. Only the framing changed: losing five cents versus gaining five cents.

cards.title: Loss aversion
body: **Loss aversion** means a loss feels stronger than a gain of the same size. In many studies, losing something hurts roughly twice as much as gaining it pleases.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described it in 1979. People judge outcomes against a starting point, and dropping below that point weighs more than rising above it.
A bag fee drops shoppers below their starting point. A bonus nudges them slightly above it.

image.label: Lopsided scale: a small loss outweighs an equal gain
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Lose $5", 오른쪽 접시에 "Gain $5". 같은 금액인데 왼쪽이 훨씬 아래로 기울어짐. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.softwareNote: This is why ending a free trial by removing features a user already set up stings more than inviting them to upgrade. "You'll lose your saved projects" moves people more than "Unlock more projects."

cards.title: Once it's yours, it's worth more.
body: In a 1990 experiment, Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler gave coffee mugs to half the people in a room. Owners then asked for about **twice as much** to sell their mug as others were willing to pay for it.
Nothing about the mug changed. Owning it moved the starting point, so giving it up felt like a loss.
The same logic shows up in business: a perk customers already have, a feature they already use, a price they're already paying.

cards.title: It works inside your company too.
body: Employees react to losing a perk, a budget line or a desk by the window far more strongly than they'd value gaining the same thing.
That's why a reorganization that is fair on paper can still feel like theft. People count what they gave up in full and discount what they got in return.
Leaders often explain changes in terms of total value. Teams hear the list of losses first.

cards.title: Not every loss looms large.
body: The effect is strongest when people feel something is truly theirs. Spending money they expected to spend, like paying a normal bill, often doesn't feel like a loss at all. Some researchers argue the effect is smaller and more situational than the famous "twice as much" suggests.
And framing can turn into manipulation. Inventing losses, like fake countdown timers or made-up "last items," may work once. Customers notice, and trust is the bigger loss.

cards.title: Now you're changing your team's schedule.
body: You lead a 12-person operations team at a large company. Leadership wants to replace the team's Friday half-day with flexible hours across the week. On paper, the total time off is the same.
How do you roll it out?

options.text: Announce it plainly: Friday half-days end next month, flexible hours start
options.feedback: Clear and fast. But people will hear "we're taking your Friday" first, and the equal gain will feel smaller than the loss.

options.text: Offer a small one-time bonus to make up for the change
options.feedback: It shows you see the cost. But because losses weigh more, a small gain rarely offsets taking away something people already own.

options.text: Let people keep Fridays if they want, and offer flex hours as an option to try for a month
options.feedback: Nobody loses anything they have, so resistance drops. You give up a quick, uniform switch, but many may choose flex hours once they've tried it.

cards.title: People fight harder to keep than to gain.
body: Before any change, ask what it looks like from the customer's or employee's starting point. What will they feel they are losing?
**Try it today:** pick one change you're planning, like a price, a policy or a feature. Write down everything someone could feel they lose, then find one way to let them keep it.
